title: 631. Leadership Communication Is All About Repetition
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This issue argues that repeating a message is not redundant but a deliberate leadership strategy, especially during organizational change, because a message shared three or four times only starts to feel exhausting to the leader, not fully internalized by the team. It backs the claim with on-record habits from Indra Nooyi (touring every PepsiCo division quarterly to repeat priorities), Marc Benioff (broadcasting values across every channel to avoid 'message dilution'), and Howard Schultz (returning to Starbucks' mission and values from scratch on every visit). It closes with research-backed framing from Adam Grant, who notes reactions to an idea typically improve after ten to twenty exposures, and from The CEO Next Door, which puts the number at seven repetitions in seven different forms before an organization truly hears a message.
points: The core argument reframes repetition as strategy rather than redundancy: leaders who feel like 'a broken record' after three or four repetitions are usually still far short of full team internalization.

Indra Nooyi's discipline of touring every PepsiCo division at least quarterly to repeat the company's purpose and priorities is offered as the model behavior: 'Repetition builds alignment—and alignment is everything.'
Adam Grant's research citation quantifies the threshold: reactions to an unconventional idea typically become more positive only after ten to twenty exposures.
The CEO Next Door research puts a harder number on organizational communication: a message must be repeated seven times in seven different ways before an organization has any real hope of hearing it.
quotes: If there's one communication principle leaders underestimate, it's this: repetition isn't a redundancy - it's strategy.
I would go to every division at least every quarter and repeat the purpose and priorities of PepsiCo. Repetition builds alignment—and alignment is everything.
It's not enough to say your values once. You have to broadcast them constantly—internal town halls, customer meetings, social media. Message dilution is leadership failure.
You have to say it over and over and over again. Every time I came back to Starbucks, I started with the basics. The mission, the values, the why.
Make your ideas more familiar. Repeat yourself—it makes people more comfortable with an unconventional idea. Reactions typically become more positive after ten to twenty exposures to an idea.
Any message has to be repeated seven times in seven different ways before an organization has any hope of hearing it.
